newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar on tenterhooks for wage news.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar on tenterhooks for wage news.

text.p: The Australian dollar froze at midday as the market anxiously awaited news on a national minimum wage claim with implications for monetary policy.

The Industrial Relations Commission will hand down its verdict on the union claim at 2.00 pm and the market has priced in an award equivalent to around A$12 a week. Any less or more will be seen as, respectively, increasing or decreasing the chance of a rate cut and would tend to hurt or aid the dollar.
Elsewhere, the impact of the Victorian power station sale was fast fading as much of the price was being met by debt raised here and any forex exposure looked to have been covered.
By 12.00 pm (0200 GMT) the local dollar was on edge at US$0.7777/82 having barely stirred from its early US$0.7770/75 and Monday's late US$0.7765/70.

Support was well defined at US$0.7720 after surviving a few days of downside pressure, while resistance was proving stubborn in the US$0.7785/95 band. A break of either was expected to trigger a quick stop-loss move with US$0.7680 and US$0.7820 the immediate targets in each case.
As many dealers had suspected, the forex effect of the power sale was limited by the fact that a great part of the payment -- around A$3.6 billion -- was funded by debt raised in Australia.
A source close to the deal said the exposure to the A$ was only around A$500 million and dealers reckoned most of that had already been covered.

The Living Wage case had the potential for a much longer lasting impact through its effect on inflation and monetary policy. The union claim was for an 8.75 percent increase in award wages and three annual A$20 per week pay rises for the lower paid. The government argued for a rise of just A$8 a week. The Reserve Bank warned that granting the full claim would add around 1.6 percentage points to wages growth, threaten the maintenance of low inflation and add to unemployment.
In such a case, the bank said, it might ultimately have to take policy action to redress the situation.
Analysts felt this warning alone should have tempered the IRC's decision and most expected a flat weekly rise of A$10-A$15 a week and no percentage increase in award wages.
However, assessing the outcome could be complicated if the IRC grants a mixture of weekly and percentage rises, so the market might take time to react fully.
On the crosses, the dollar had edged up to 97.70/80 yen from 97.45/55 and to 60.1 in trade weighted terms from 60.0.
